Three patterns for automation: CI review, scheduled device health checks, and log summarization. Adapt paths, devices, and model settings before production use.
GitHub Actions example using @dmoss/agent on a PR diff:

# .github/workflows/review.yml
name: AI Code Review

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '22'

      - name: Install @dmoss/agent
        run: npm install -g @dmoss/agent

      - name: Review diff
        env:
          DMOSS_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.DMOSS_API_KEY }}
          DMOSS_MODEL: claude-sonnet-4-20250514
          DMOSS_BASE_URL: https://api.anthropic.com
        run: |
          git diff origin/main HEAD | dmoss-agent --pipe \
            "review the diff, focus on bugs and missing tests"
dmoss-agent interprets the diff, flags likely bugs, and suggests tests—output lands in Action logs.

# /etc/cron.d/rdk-checkin
0 * * * * rdkstudio exec "df -h /; free -h; uptime" --device prod-x5-01 \

Disk, memory, and uptime append each hour—scan the log for trends.

#!/bin/bash
# /opt/rdk/daily-health.sh
set -e

DIAGNOSIS=$(rdkstudio exec "cat /proc/meminfo; df -h; dmesg | tail -100" --device prod-x5-01)

echo "$DIAGNOSIS" | dmoss-agent --pipe \
  "Analyze this device output and give a health score plus recommendations" \
  > /var/log/rdk-daily-report.log

journalctl -u myservice --since="1 hour ago" \
  | dmoss-agent --pipe "summarize errors and root causes"
dmoss-agent clusters issues and suggests causes—handy when logs are huge.

LOG=$(journalctl -u myservice --since="5m ago" --no-pager)

RESULT=$(echo "$LOG" | dmoss-agent --pipe --json \
  "Check for severe errors. Return JSON: {severity: none|low|medium|high, summary: '...'}")

SEVERITY=$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '.severity')

if [ "$SEVERITY" = "high" ]; then
  curl -X POST https://your-alert-endpoint \
    -d "$(echo "$RESULT" | jq -r '.summary')"
fi

After switching pages, return to the workbench or the left task list to continue. Provide logs, files, or diagnostics as attachments or references when asking for analysis, so the Agent has the relevant material.
Board offline: keep its project binding and saved information; restore the intended device before operating.
No folder selected: bind the appropriate folder through the project or workspace entry.
Runtime unavailable: open settings and recheck. Changing the default requires creating a new task.
Task running: check its state before adding instructions, stopping, or starting another task to avoid duplicate execution.

Use the device label, work-location bar, and task overview to confirm the intended target and connection state. Before diagnosis, verify the project's bound device rather than assuming another online device is the target.

Read-only: check the bound device's model, system version, CPU, memory, disk, temperature, network, and key services. State any missing information. Do not change configuration or restart anything.

The Agent gathers information using tools available to its runtime. Fields vary by board, OS, permissions, and connection. Inspect the reason for missing information; a missing field does not mean the entire device is unavailable.

Review problems, evidence, and suggestions in the answer. Open existing execution records from the message's more menu if needed. Preserve command failures, timeouts, and missing-field messages; they are not a successful diagnosis.
Offline snapshots describe previously collected information. Working local files or terminals do not prove that the board connection has recovered.

When the device is offline or the network is unstable, the Workbench does not go blank—it shows the last fetched state and marks the device offline. That way you can still gauge what was happening before the device dropped.
